claims_draft:
# Draft claims, UFO follow-up on Qwen3-1.7B (to be attacked; nothing here is final)

Setting: Qwen3-1.7B chat model, CPU, fp32. 16 texts (8 wikitext passages, 8 chats = question + answer of a fine-tuned model),
64 tokens each; positions from the fifth on, chat-template tokens excluded. A vector delta is added to the residual stream.
Size f times the norm of the state. Direction classes: cov (Gaussian with the covariance of real states at that block),
irr (random vector outside the principal subspace that holds 98 % of the variance of held-out real states, mean direction
removed), mix (difference of two real states), rand (isotropic). Pool of real states: 192 other texts (ufo_pool.py).
"Local" rows: after EVERY block the state is reset to clean + fresh vector, and the reaction of the next block is read.
q = -<write difference of the block, delta> / |delta|^2. Intervals: 95 % bootstrap over texts.

C1  On running text the states are not low-dimensional: 98 % of the variance of held-out states needs 1654-1837 of 2048
    principal axes (blocks 0-21); 8 axes hold 14-15 %; two real states are 1.06-1.21 state norms apart (median).
C2  Local erasure q per block (f = 0.3), mean over responding blocks 1-4 / 5-10 / 11-16 / 17-22 / 23-26:
    cov 0.111 / 0.130 / 0.049 / 0.002 / 0.007; irr 0.213 / 0.209 / 0.152 / 0.043 / 0.018; rand 0.196 / 0.206 / 0.101 / 0.031 / 0.015;
    mix 0.111 / 0.124 / 0.040 / -0.001 / 0.007. Contrast irr - cov: +0.102 [0.101, 0.103] / +0.078 / +0.102 / +0.042 / +0.012.
    The attention part is at most 0.025; the rest comes from the MLP.
C3  No brake for large vectors: q(0.3)/q(0.03) = 0.97 (cov), 0.945 (irr); q(1)/q(0.03) = 0.75 (cov), 0.59 (irr); RMSNorm
    alone predicts 0.958 and 0.707. Output KL grows with log-log slope 2.0 between 0.03 and 0.3 and 2.1-2.6 between 0.3 and 1.
    Hence neither a plateau for small vectors nor a mechanism that sets in for large ones.
C4  Free run from block 2, f = 0.3: of an irr vector 80 % is left after one block, 32 % after four, 5 % at the end; cov: 88 %,
    65 %, 130 % at the end. The absolute deviation grows 37-44 fold (the stream about 100 fold), so the relative deviation
    falls to 0.39-0.48 of its start value. Two blocks after an irr vector was added, 89 % of the deviation lies inside the data subspace.
C5  The erasure protects the output. With the component along delta removed from every later attention and MLP write (A):
    KL 0.071 -> 0.143 for irr at block 2 (ratio 2.01 [1.70, 2.42]); cov at block 2: 0.111 -> 0.143 (1.29 [1.22, 1.36]);
    block 14: irr 1.33 [1.30, 1.38], cov 0.90 [0.88, 0.92]. Without erasure cov and irr cost the same (0.143 / 0.143 and
    0.075 / 0.074). With only the erasure kept (B), or the vector riding along untouched, KL stays below 0.002: the damage is
    carried by the part of the blocks' reaction that is orthogonal to delta.
C6  The erasure is local: a vector at one position gives KL 0.07-0.18 at that position and 0.001-0.008 at later positions;
    the share left after 1 and 4 blocks is the same as with vectors at all positions. One and the same vector at all
    positions costs 1.3-2.3 times more KL than independent vectors of the same size.
C7  The final deviation of an early vector costs 1.5-2.3 times the KL of a random vector of the same final size added after
    the last block. Under noise the entropy rises at least as much as the loss (dLoss - dH = -0.69 [-0.99, -0.40] for cov,
    f = 1, block 2); most of that rise is carried by the final norm (dH 1.84 -> 0.38 with the clean scale). Zeroing the MLP
    of block 2: loss +7.6, entropy -0.78.
C8  At equal relative size 0.3 the output KL is similar for vectors added after blocks 0 / 2 / 8 / 14 (cov 0.078 / 0.111 /
    0.080 / 0.083; irr 0.053 / 0.071 / 0.062 / 0.055): the lowest blocks are neither clearly more tolerant nor more fragile.
C9  Mechanism (ufo_lin.py, exact first-order formula, one clean pass): the formula reproduces the measured local erasure
    (blocks 1-4: irr 0.194 + attention 0.024 against 0.214 measured; cov 0.103 + 0.008 against 0.111). With the output
    weights assigned to the wrong neurons the erasure is 0.000. In blocks 1-9 it runs through the up projection (not the
    gate), comes from neurons whose gate input is negative at that position (85-98 % of the neurons; 0.16-0.25 against
    about -0.01 from neurons with positive gate input), and more from the weakest three quarters of the neurons than from
    the strongest quarter; 800-1800 neurons carry half of it. Mean cosine between the up-projection weight and the output
    weight of a neuron: +0.16 to +0.34 in blocks 1-9. From block 10 on neurons with positive gate input take over.
    Reading: SiLU is slightly negative for negative input, so an inactive neuron passes its up input with a small negative
    factor; with output weight aligned to the read direction this is a weak negative feedback, spread over thousands of neurons.
C10 Qwen-Scope SAEs (TopK, 32768 units, k = 50, trained on the BASE model) explain 88 / 83 / 70 / 63 / 76 % of the variance at
    blocks 0 / 2 / 8 / 14 / 21 on these texts (chat-model SAE at block 21: 83 %). 90-95 % of the error energy lies inside the
    data subspace. The SAE reconstruction is hardly more compressible than the state (held-out share in 128 axes at block 2:
    29 % against 27 %; error 17 %): the SAE does not move the state towards a low-dimensional geometry.
C11 Replacing the state by its SAE reconstruction at one block: KL 0.066 / 0.142 / 0.221 / 0.301 / 0.299 (blocks 0 / 2 / 8 / 14 / 21;
    chat-model SAE at 21: 0.203). Relative to cov noise of the same size: 0.65 / 0.94 / 1.15 / 1.37 / 1.26; to irr noise:
    0.94 / 1.09 / 1.49 / 1.79 / 2.02. PCA with the same explained variance costs 2-3 times the SAE. An error vector of another
    state of the same size costs as much at block 0 (0.072) and half as much at block 14 (0.156 against 0.301).
C12 What the splice removes is erased like noise at blocks 0-2 (share left after four blocks 0.48 / 0.42; irr 0.36 / 0.32,
    cov 0.74 / 0.64) and kept like content from block 14 on (1.06).
C13 Clean pass, no intervention: later blocks write ALONG the part of the state the SAE does not explain, more than along
    the explained part (sum of coefficients 22 against 18 at block 0, 26 against 7 at block 2, 7.6 against 3.3 at block 8).
    The part of the clean state outside the data subspace gets -0.40 / -0.42 / -0.32 over the next four blocks (inside part
    +0.36 / +0.11 / +0.38, random vector 0.00).
C14 SAE as a filter: of noise of size 0.3 |h| it passes 38-42 % at blocks 0 / 2 (51-58 % at block 14), the same for cov and irr;
    75-82 % of the active units stay active. Without its own error it leaves 20-27 % of the noise's KL at blocks 0 / 2
    (44-48 % at 14). In real time (its own error included) SAE(h + d) gives KL 0.078 against 0.081 for the noise alone at
    block 0, 0.155 against 0.091 at block 2, 0.330 against 0.085 at block 14.
C15 The UFO paper's own criterion on Qwen (z-scored MLP activations at the last prompt token, 1472 DSSE prompts, fit on two
    thirds, read on the held-out third): 2 principal axes explain 32-39 % in blocks 0-8, falling to 9-11 % in blocks 23-26;
    a 2-dim non-linear autoencoder 28-38 % held-out. But the first axis is the prompt length in blocks 0-2 (R^2 0.83-0.87)
    and the question family from block 3 on (0.81-0.95), and the 18 families alone explain 31-48 % of the variance of all
    neurons. The figure describes the prompt set.

Interpretation offered:
I1  There is something in the forward pass that removes what does not belong: a generic negative feedback by the MLPs of the
    lower two thirds of the network, twice as strong for directions outside the data subspace, which halves the output
    damage of such vectors added at block 2. It is not an organiser in the sense of the UFO paper (which acts only during
    training): not low-dimensional, no separate component, linear in the size of the vector, no threshold, and carried by
    the bulk of weakly active neurons rather than by a few identifiable ones.
I2  A 'safety mechanism that brakes when the disturbance gets too large' was not found (C3).
I3  For an SAE in the loop the lowest block is the cheapest place. As a filter the SAE helps only if its own reconstruction
    error is put back (read, modify, write back the difference).
I4  Whether training produced the erasure (random-initialised control) and whether a model that keeps only its strongest
    neuron activations loses it are being computed.

result.verdict:
All headline numbers of C9 to C14 reproduce from the stored outputs with my own code. C15 reproduces except for three ranges. The first-order formula in ufo_lin.py is correct. The problems are in readings, not in arithmetic.

Stands as written: the C9 formula and its agreement with the measured local erasure; the KL values and noise ratios of C11; the downstream shares of C12; the second sentence of C13; the three KLs of C14; the core of C15 (the two axes describe the prompt set).

Needs change:
- **C11, PCA:** the comparison is not at equal explained variance. On the texts PCA explains 6 to 15 points less than the SAE in 12 of 12 texts at every site. At equal unexplained energy "2-3 times" becomes about 1.2 to 1.9 times, and at blocks 0 and 2 it is not clearly above 1.
- **C13, first sentence:** "22 against 18, 26 against 7, 7.6 against 3.3" comes from blocks 22-26. Up to block 21 the order is equal or reversed, and in the next four blocks the unexplained part is written against. The coefficients are a clean-pass correlation, not a reaction of the blocks.
- **C14, "passes 38-42 %":** this is the size of the change of the SAE output. Its cosine with the noise is 0.10 to 0.20, so 4 to 8 % of the noise passes along its own direction. The draft quotes only cov for the real-time KL; for irr at block 0 the SAE in real time is worse than the noise alone.
- **I3:** the "error put back" row uses the error of the clean state, which is not available at run time.
- **C12, "kept like content":** cov noise is kept just as well at block 14.
- **C9, reading:** "inactive" is not shown, and the reading holds for blocks 1-9 only.
- **C10:** "90-95 % inside the data subspace" lacks its baseline (an isotropic vector has 81 to 90 %), and block 2 is the block with the smallest compressibility gap.
- **C15:** three ranges are off (see the table), and the held-out autoencoder figure depends on training length.

Not recomputed: the autoencoder numbers (taken from ufo_compress.json) and the compress figures of C10 (taken from the stored pool statistics). The length and family R^2 of C15 exist only for blocks 0-11 in the partial log; I spot-checked nine blocks with my own code, using character count as a proxy for token length.

No model was loaded. Every call ran pinned to core 3 at nice 19; the largest read one 18 MB block of neu_act.npy at a time (3-4 s per block). My scripts and one output file are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-DSSE/85db304a-b0fa-5d03-b685-f9acf8fac842/scratchpad/ufo_review/checker_c9c15/ (a1_lin.py, a2_split.py, b1_sae_sites.py, b2_bcoef.py, b2_bcoef.out, b3_bcoef_identity.py, b4_pca_axes.py, b5_sites_paired.py, c1_cross_compress.py, c2_compress_check.py). No existing file was modified.

findings.claim: C9 / check (1): ufo_lin.py implements the exact first-order formula for Qwen3's MLP, including the radial term, the three direction classes, the pool statistics of block m-1 and the permuted control.
findings.evidence: Own derivation: x = gamma*h/rms with rms = |h|/sqrt(D), so dx = (gamma/rms)*(delta - hhat (hhat.delta)). With a_n = silu(u_n) v_n: da_n = silu'(u_n) v_n W_gate[n].dx + silu(u_n) W_up[n].dx, and W_gate[n].(gamma*hhat) = u_n/sqrt(D), W_up[n].(gamma*hhat) = v_n/sqrt(D). Hence E[c_n] = -(1/rms) [ silu'(u_n) v_n (G_n^T M w_n - (u_n/sqrt(D)) hhat^T M w_n) + silu(u_n) (B_n^T M w_n - (v_n/sqrt(D)) hhat^T M w_n) ], G_n = gamma*W_gate[n], B_n = gamma*W_up[n]. Lines 32, 40-41 and 49-52 compute exactly this; dsilu is correct; the hooks capture the gate and up outputs and the input of post_attention_layernorm. M: rand I/D; irr QQ^T/(D-k) with Q an orthonormal basis of the axes beyond k_irr after removing the mean direction (same construction as Pool.direction); cov U diag(sd^2) U^T / sum(sd^2). Block m uses P.b[m-1], matching the local rows of ufo_damp2.py. The split is computed as described: gate path, up path, gate input < 0, >= 0, strongest quarter of |silu(u) v| at the position, rest; each pair adds up to km within 6e-8. Small points: (a) the permuted control (cp, line 52) leaves out the radial term; (b) for cov, unit vectors of a Gaussian do not have exactly covariance/trace as second moment, an effect of at most about 1 % given participation ratios of 157-209; (c) ufo_lin.log (23:09) is older than ufo_lin.npz / .json (23:11) and holds no split table; its first table agrees with the npz.
findings.fix: Say that the permuted control omits the radial term, or add it. Keep the log of the run that wrote the npz, since the split numbers of the draft can only be traced to ufo_lin.npz. None of this changes a conclusion.

findings.claim: C9 / check (2): the formula reproduces the measured local erasure (blocks 1-4: irr 0.194 + attention 0.024 against 0.214; cov 0.103 + 0.008 against 0.111).
findings.evidence: Band values reproduce: irr 0.1944 + 0.0244 = 0.2188 against q_tot 0.2139 (f = 0.03); cov 0.1032 + 0.0082 = 0.1114 against 0.1110. MLP alone: irr 0.1944 against q_mlp 0.1894 (-2.6 %), cov 0.1032 against 0.1029, rand 0.1827 against 0.1792. Per block, measured q_mlp(0.03) minus formula over blocks 1-27: rand rms 0.0034, largest -0.0114 at block 9 (-6.0 %); irr rms 0.0037, largest -0.0109 at block 11 (-6.4 %); cov rms 0.0058, largest -0.0244 at block 14 (0.0631 against 0.0876, -28 %, sd over texts 0.0037, 95 % interval [-0.026, -0.023]). Correlation over blocks 0.9996 / 0.9995 / 0.9962. Attention in between: for rand and irr the differences follow -km_lin * q_att (attention removes the share q_att of the vector before the MLP reads it): fitted slope 0.90 / 0.97, residual rms after that correction 0.0017 / 0.0011. For cov the same correction leaves rms 0.0053 and -0.021 at block 14, so it does not explain cov. Non-linearity cannot explain a gap at f = 0.03: the second-order term cancels for sign-symmetric directions, and the deviation measured between 0.03 and 0.3 at block 14 (q_mlp 0.0631 -> 0.0499, 17 % beyond RMSNorm) scales to about 0.2 % at 0.03. What remains for cov at block 14 is the part of the attention write that is not parallel to the vector and is then read by the MLP; this is an inference, not a measurement. At f = 0.3 there is non-linearity beyond RMSNorm: measured / (km_lin (1 - q_att) / sqrt(1.09)) is 1.03-1.06 in blocks 1-4 and 0.91-0.99 in blocks 5-16 (rand, irr); cov block 14: 0.63.
findings.fix: State the agreement per block (rand and irr within 6.4 % everywhere, within about 1 % after the attention correction) and name the exception cov at block 14 (-28 %). To close it: one local row with the attention write of the block held at its clean value, or the closed form with the attention Jacobian. The conclusion of C9 is unchanged.

findings.claim: C9: in blocks 1-9 the erasure runs through the up projection, comes from neurons with negative gate input (85-98 % of the neurons; 0.16-0.25 against about -0.01), more from the weakest three quarters than from the strongest quarter; from block 10 on neurons with positive gate input take over.
findings.evidence: irr, blocks 1-9, from ufo_lin.npz: gate path +0.007 to +0.012, up path +0.145 to +0.237. Gate input < 0: +0.160 to +0.254; >= 0: -0.011 to +0.017 (blocks 1-7: -0.007 to -0.011; block 8: -0.001; block 9: +0.017). Share of neurons with negative gate input 0.837-0.975, i.e. 84-98 %, not 85-98 %. Strongest quarter +0.055 to +0.080, rest +0.072 to +0.170; in block 1 the strongest quarter carries more than the rest (0.080 against 0.072; same order for rand and cov). Per neuron the strongest quarter contributes 1.09 to 3.35 times as much as a neuron of the rest in every block 1-9, and it carries 27-53 % of the erasure with 25 % of the neurons. Take-over: share of positive-gate neurons for irr is 28 % at block 10, 46 % at block 11, 64 % at block 12 (rand crosses at block 12, cov at block 11). The stored split has only the marginals (path; gate sign), not the four cells path x gate sign, so 'negative-gate neurons through the up path' is inferred from two marginals.
findings.fix: Write 84-98 %; '-0.011 to +0.017 from neurons with positive gate input'; 'in blocks 2-9 more in total from the weakest three quarters, per neuron the strongest quarter contributes 1.1 to 3.4 times as much'; 'positive-gate neurons carry the larger part from block 12 on'. Add the joint split path x gate sign to ufo_lin.py (one more pass of about a minute). The main statement (up path, negative gate input, many neurons) stands.

findings.claim: C9 reading / check (3): 'SiLU is slightly negative for negative input, so an inactive neuron passes its up input with a small negative factor; with output weight aligned to the read direction this is a weak negative feedback'.
findings.evidence: Consistent with the numbers for blocks 1-9: mean cos(up, down) +0.1605 to +0.3397, 74-94 % of the neurons above +0.1 (chance sd 0.022), 84-98 % negative gate input, up path 93-97 % of the total. The simpler statement behind it is a sign rule: to first order a neuron contributes -silu(u_n) * B_n^T M w_n / rms, so it erases when its gate value and its up/down alignment have opposite signs. In blocks 1-7 positive-gate neurons amplify by a similar amount per neuron (-5.1 to -1.2 e-5 against +2.7 to +4.5 e-5 for negative-gate neurons); the net is erasure because nearly all gates are negative. Three things the data do not show. (1) 'Inactive': the gate-input distribution is not stored; SiLU's negative lobe reaches -0.278 at u = -1.28, and per neuron the strongest quarter by |activation| contributes more than the rest. (2) Alignment beyond blocks 1-9: in blocks 12-16 the mean cosine is +0.03 to -0.06 while the irr erasure is still 0.13-0.18; it is then carried by positive-gate neurons through the up path, which requires anti-aligned up and output weights (30-40 % of neurons below -0.1). The correlation over blocks between mean cosine and erasure (+0.90 irr, +0.94 rand) is therefore partly a depth trend. (3) The relevant alignment is B_n^T M w_n with gamma, per class and per gate sign; the json has the plain cosine of the raw weights over all neurons. The mean cos(gate, down) of 0 says nothing: flipping the sign of a neuron's up row and output column leaves the network unchanged and flips that cosine.
findings.fix: Replace 'inactive neuron' by 'neuron with negative gate input (gate value between -0.28 and 0)' and limit the reading to blocks 1-9. To make it safe add: the four-cell split, the mean silu(u) and the mean B_n^T M w_n of negative-gate and positive-gate neurons separately, and one sentence on blocks 12-16. The mechanism claim itself (first-order, checked against measurement) stands.

findings.claim: C9: '800-1800 neurons carry half of it' (check 1: does 'neurons for half of the erasure' mean what the draft says?).

result.verdict:
Numbers: they stand. I re-derived 23 quantities of C1-C15 with my own code from the stored outputs. None is wrong; two ranges are slightly off (C1: 8 axes hold 13-18 %, not 14-15 %; C15: 31-40 % and 8-10 % held-out) and neither changes a conclusion. Interpretation: I1 and I3 do not stand as worded, I2 stands with a narrower scope, I4 is largely answered by files written after the draft.

Supported by the tables: training gave the MLPs of blocks 1-16 a linear, unspecific contraction that the untrained network lacks (q = 0.000 there). A block writes against any added vector with a coefficient near 0.2 in blocks 1-10, and near 0.11 along the few hundred directions of highest data variance.

Not supported, by the six points of the task:
(a) A safety mechanism. The erasure is learned, but it has none of the marks that would separate protection from ordinary computation. It does not depend on size, it is not selective for foreign directions, and it does not bring the state back: in all 34 plain free rows the deviation is 1.07-1.28 times the added vector one block later and never below 1.04 afterwards; the erasure is 3-8 % of the energy of a block's reaction. The 'protection' in test A equals the squared ratio of the final deviations (2.01 against 2.01): a vector that stays is read again. In vector size the margin is 1.42 for irr at block 2 and 0.95 for cov at block 14.
(b) 'Twice as strong outside the data subspace' follows from the energy distribution of the classes. A generic direction inside the 98 % subspace gets 0.19-0.21, like one outside; cov has 56-70 % of its energy on 256 axes; mix has the same second moment as cov and is no second witness. At the output irr and isotropic vectors cost the same (1.03 [0.89, 1.21]).
(c) C9's reading is right as arithmetic and too strong in three words ('inactive', 'feedback', 'weak'). It covers blocks 1-9; in blocks 10-16 positive-gate neurons with opposed weights give the same sign.
(d) Every SAE statement for blocks 0-14 is about base-model SAEs on the chat model. At block 21 the chat-model SAE costs 0.68 [0.62, 0.76] of the KL and the part it leaves unexplained is written along half as much (0.095 against 0.188). 'The error is content' and the depth profile behind I3 are partly properties of the mismatch.
(e) The claims are single passes. They cannot show accumulation, run-to-run difference or the effect of a purposeful write. A loop run on disk (12 prompts, 32 greedy tokens; not in the claims) shows no growth of the per-token KL and a changed text in 12 of 12 prompts for every SAE row.
(f) One model for everything. Solid within it: q (a replicate draw agrees to 0.002). Carried by one draw and few positions: every KL (row means of two draws differ by up to 22 %; the top tenth of positions carries 42-54 % of a row's KL).

Three further points: C13 leaves out two sites with the opposite sign (+0.19 at block 14, +0.22 at block 21) and the long horizon (+4.2 for block 2). I3's 'helps if its own error is put back' needs the undisturbed state and cannot be built. C14 quotes only the noise class for which the SAE breaks even.

The last finding holds a proposed paragraph for the user on H1 and H2.

findings.claim: C2 and point (b): contrast irr - cov read as 'twice as strong for directions outside the data subspace'. Could it follow from how the classes are built?
findings.evidence: Yes, in three ways. (1) Energy distribution. To first order the local q of a class depends only on its second-moment matrix. cov puts 13-18 % of its energy on 8 axes, 35-44 % on 64 and 56-70 % on 256; an isotropic vector inside the 98 % subspace puts 14 % on the top 256. My own solve from the rand and irr rows reproduces Recomputation A: generic inside direction 0.192 [0.187, 0.196] / 0.206 / 0.093 / 0.029 / 0.014 at f = 0.3, against irr 0.213 / 0.209 / 0.152 / 0.043 / 0.018. Inside minus cov is +0.081 / +0.076 / +0.043, that is 79 % of the contrast in blocks 1-4, 96 % in blocks 5-10, 42 % in blocks 11-16. cov cannot say how many directions are spared: 14 % of the energy on axes with coefficient -0.4 and the rest at 0.2 gives 0.116, the same as a smooth gradient. (2) mix is no second witness. It has the same second moment as cov, so 0.111 / 0.124 / 0.040 next to 0.111 / 0.130 / 0.049 is linearity, not confirmation by real content. rand is a mixture of the other two. C2 holds three independent numbers per band, not four. (3) Subspace definition. 'Outside' is the 10-19 % of axes with least variance (211-394 dimensions). Real states have a component there of about 0.12 state norms (block 2: sqrt(0.02) x 1.165 / sqrt(2) = 0.116). An irr vector at f = 0.03 is a quarter of that, at 0.3 it is 2.6 times as large; both are erased alike (0.214 and 0.213 in blocks 1-4). The coefficient does not depend on whether the vector exceeds what the data contain. The mean direction plays no role: radial share 0.006-0.009 for cov, below 0.0001 for irr, 0.0005 for rand. At the output the classes separate less than in q: KL irr / cov 0.68 [0.57, 0.80] (block 2) and 0.72 [0.62, 0.82] (block 14) with both direction draws averaged; irr / rand 1.03 [0.89, 1.21] and 1.04 [0.93, 1.16]; final relative deviation irr / cov 0.82 [0.72, 0.93]. First-order split (ufo_lin.npz): in blocks 1-9 the cov - irr difference lies in the same term as the erasure itself. By gate sign: negative-gate neurons -0.100 of -0.091 (blocks 1-4) and -0.082 of -0.080 (blocks 5-9), positive-gate +0.009 and +0.002. By path: up path -0.091 and -0.069. It is a weaker read-write alignment along high-variance directions, not a second process that writes content back.
findings.fix: Replace 'outside the data subspace' by 'every direction except those of highest data variance'. findings.claim: C5 and point (a): 'The erasure protects the output'. Learned safety mechanism or by-product of ordinary computation?
findings.evidence: Learned: yes. In the randomly initialised network (ufo_damp2_randinit.npz, same 16 texts, written after the draft) q is 0.000 in every band and class (largest single block 0.002) and the share left stays 1.00. A safety mechanism: nothing in the tables requires it, and seven observations fit ordinary computation at least as well. (1) Linear, no threshold (C3). (2) Not selective for foreign directions (finding on C2). (3) Not restoring: every block adds more deviation than it removes (finding on C4). (4) Test A changes only the size of the final deviation. KL ratio A / normal against the ratio of the mean squared final relative deviation: 2.01 against 2.01 [1.85, 2.21] (irr, block 2), 1.29 against 1.23, 1.33 against 1.33, 0.90 against 0.90; KL per squared deviation 3.61 and 3.60. A vector that stays is read again by every block; the test shows no more than that. In size the margin is small: for equal KL the vector may be 1.42 times larger (irr, block 2), 1.15 (irr, 14), 1.13 (cov, 2), 0.95 (cov, 14). (5) The blocks react to both classes alike: orthogonal reaction per unit 0.72-0.82 (irr) and 0.63-0.84 (cov) in blocks 1-16. Low-variance directions are read as much as high-variance ones, which fits 'without erasure cov and irr cost the same'. (6) q does not set the damage. With the weaker half of the neuron activations zeroed (top0.5 run, same draws as the replicate run) q stays at 0.95 while the KL of block-2 vectors rises 1.35 [1.10, 1.60] / 1.48 [1.19, 1.84] / 1.68 [1.51, 1.87] (cov / irr / rand). The untrained network, with q = 0, has KL 0.086 at block 2 and 0.045 at block 14, the same order as the trained one (0.067-0.111 and 0.055-0.083); its output is near uniform, so this is an indication only. (7) Without any vector, the next four blocks write against the low-variance part of the model's own state at blocks 0, 2 and 8 (-0.40 / -0.42 / -0.32); the contraction is part of ordinary processing there. 'B below 0.002' is no finding about the erasure: the untouched vector is 0.003 of the final norm (0.3 x 27.8 / 2714).
findings.fix: Write: 'Keeping the vector in the stream makes the final deviation 1.42 times larger and the KL twice as large for irr at block 2 (1.33 in KL at block 14; cov 1.29 and 0.90). The erasure shortens the time a vector is read. It is learned; whether for robustness or as part of ordinary processing these runs cannot tell.' A test that could tell: set the negative lobe of SiLU to zero in blocks 1-9 (C9 says it carries the erasure) and compare clean loss and noise KL. If the clean loss holds and only the noise KL rises, the erasure serves robustness; if the clean loss breaks, it is ordinary computation.

findings.claim: C9 and point (c): is 'an inactive neuron passes its up input with a small negative factor ... a weak negative feedback, spread over thousands of neurons' the simplest reading?
findings.evidence: The arithmetic is the simplest possible, and Recomputation B confirmed it: to first order a neuron contributes minus its gate value silu(u) times the product of its up weight and its output weight (read through the class), a linear path whose gain is the gate value. Three words go beyond that. 'Inactive': the path needs a gate value clearly below zero (SiLU is -0.07 at u = -4 and -0.28 at u = -1.28); a neuron that is really off contributes nothing. The outputs for the trained model hold no gate-input distribution; the bins and the stronger-half column of the current ufo_lin.py exist only in ufo_lin_randinit.npz. 'Feedback': the term is no reaction to the vector. It is a fixed linear part of the MLP that acts on the clean state as well. 'Weak': 0.2 per block leaves 0.13 after nine blocks. What the split shows (ufo_lin.npz, irr, blocks 1-9): negative-gate neurons +0.160 to +0.254, positive-gate -0.011 to +0.017, share of negative gates 0.837-0.975. From block 10 on the kind changes, not only the carrier: the mean cosine of up and output weight falls through zero at block 13 (+0.003) to -0.058 at block 16, and there the erasure of irr (0.131) is carried by positive-gate neurons (+0.129) whose up and output weights point against each other. Two different arrangements give the same sign across 16 blocks. That argues against 'an accident of SiLU's negative lobe' and for 'training makes the MLP contracting by whatever means are at hand', without saying what for.
findings.fix: Reword: 'In blocks 1-9 the MLP contains a linear term through neurons with negative gate value (84-98 % of the neurons) whose up and output weights are aligned (mean cosine +0.16 to +0.34). In blocks 10-16 the same sign comes from positive-gate neurons with opposed weights.' Store the bins and the stronger-half column for the trained model (one minute). Decisive between by-product and function: set silu(u) to zero where it is negative in blocks 1-9 and read clean loss and q.

findings.claim: I1: 'something in the forward pass that removes what does not belong: a generic negative feedback ... twice as strong for directions outside the data subspace, which halves the output damage of such vectors ... carried by the bulk of weakly active neurons'
findings.evidence: Five phrases do not survive the tables. 'Removes': after every block and in every row the deviation is larger than the vector (1.07-1.28 one block later, never below 1.04 afterwards); 3-8 % of a block's reaction is erasure, the rest is new deviation, and that deviation costs 1.5-2.3 times a random direction of the same size at the output (pooled; about 1.0-1.35 on the wikitext half, Recomputation A). 'What does not belong': the coefficient is the same for a vector a quarter the size of what real states carry in that subspace and for one 2.6 times larger; a generic direction inside the 98 % subspace gets 0.19-0.21. 'Twice as strong outside the data subspace': it is half as strong along the directions of highest variance; at the output irr and isotropic vectors cost the same (1.03 [0.89, 1.21]) and irr costs 0.68 [0.57, 0.80] of cov. 'Halves the output damage of such vectors': shown for irr at block 2 only (2.01); 1.33 at block 14; for cov 1.29 and 0.90; not run for rand. 'Lower two thirds' and 'bulk of weakly active neurons': for cov and mix q is 0.11-0.13 in blocks 1-10, 0.05 in blocks 11-16 and negative at block 16 (-0.068); the many-neuron picture holds for blocks 1-9 (Recomputation B); 'weakly active' is not shown, a negative gate value is not a small activation. What stands: a learned (untrained network: 0.000), linear, unspecific contraction by the MLPs, about 0.2 per block for a generic direction in blocks 1-10. On the UFO sentence: the conclusion is right for a reason that is not in the list. The paper's UFO exists only during training, so no run-time property could be one; 'not low-dimensional, no separate component, linear, no threshold' are properties of the contraction, not criteria from the paper.
findings.fix: Proposed wording: 'Training has given the MLPs of blocks 1-16 a linear contraction that the untrained network lacks: a block writes against any added vector with a coefficient of about 0.2, and about 0.11 along the few hundred directions in which real states vary most. It does not bring the state back: the block's reaction in other directions is larger than what it removes. Without it the output damage of a low-variance vector added at block 2 would be twice as large. It has no threshold and does not grow with the size of the vector. It is not the paper's organiser, which acts only during training.'

findings.claim: I2: 'A safety mechanism that brakes when the disturbance gets too large was not found (C3)'
findings.evidence: Supported within what was run. The erasure per unit falls with size (q(1) / q(0.03) = 0.75 and 0.59), the KL slope between 0.3 and 1 is 2.07-2.62, and no block shrinks the deviation at any size (size 1: 1.07-1.27 times the vector one block later). Not covered by 'not found': sizes above one state norm, a disturbance repeated over more than 32 generated tokens, other models. Two size-dependent effects exist and should be named, so that 'not found' is not read as 'looked everywhere'. The final normalisation flattens the output when the deviation adds norm (entropy rises more than loss for cov vectors of size 1 at blocks 0-8; this is arithmetic and not general, see Recomputation A). And a vector that is the same at all positions is added up by attention (finding on C6), the opposite of a brake.
findings.fix: Add 'for single disturbances of 0.03 to 1 state norm in one model'. The conclusion is unchanged.

findings.claim: I3: 'For an SAE in the loop the lowest block is the cheapest place. As a filter the SAE helps only if its own reconstruction error is put back (read, modify, write back the difference)'
findings.evidence: Second sentence. The row that 'helps' is SAE(h + d) + (h - SAE(h)). It uses the error of the undisturbed state h, which a running system does not have. With the error of the state it actually sees, SAE(h + d) + (h + d - SAE(h + d)) = h + d: the noise passes unchanged. 'Write back the difference' makes the SAE free of cost while it changes nothing, and then it is no filter. As a filter in real time the SAE is worse than the noise at blocks 2 and 14 for both classes and at block 0 for irr (finding on C14). First sentence. True for the five Qwen-Scope sites (KL 0.066 at block 0; splice / cov noise 0.65 [0.42, 1.01], splice / irr noise 0.94 [0.69, 1.33]), with five limits. It is the profile of base-model SAEs on the chat model (finding on point d). 'Cheapest' is not cheap: the top token changes at 11 % of positions, and in the loop run the text left the undisturbed text in 12 of 12 prompts (first difference at token 8.5 in the median). Cost is half of the question: what an SAE can read and write one block above the embedding was not looked at. Equal noise is not better tolerated there (C8), and a single-position vector at a low block spreads to later positions (Recomputation A). A systematic change costs 1.3-2.3 times independent noise (C6).
findings.fix: Write: 'Of the five sites tested with base-model SAEs, block 0 costs least (0.066 nats per token; top token changed at 11 % of positions). An SAE that only adds the difference between a modified and the unmodified reconstruction costs nothing while it changes nothing. Used as a filter (state replaced by the reconstruction) it does more harm than noise of 0.3 state norms at blocks 2 and 14 and breaks even at block 0 for one of two kinds of noise. Whether the lowest block is a useful place to communicate was not tested.'

A loop run is on disk but not in the claims (ufo_loop.npz: 12 prompts, 32 greedy tokens, disturbance at every token). My reading of it. The per-token KL to the clean model on the same text does not grow: slope per 10 tokens for cov noise at block 2 -0.028 [-0.064, 0.005], +0.019 [-0.002, 0.050], +0.008 (three seeds); SAE at block 0 -0.019 [-0.053, 0.001]; SAE at block 14 +0.063 [-0.045, 0.187]. findings.claim: ufo_loop.py: which positions are disturbed (bears on any use of the loop run next to C11)
findings.evidence: By reading the code. ufo_common.py marks as template the special tokens and, after each marker, the role name and line breaks; the single-pass runs neither disturb nor score them. ufo_loop.py builds its own mask from the special tokens only, and treats every generated token as valid. The loop therefore also disturbs and splices the role name and the line breaks directly before the answer, tokens that the base-model SAEs never saw in training. The consequence is visible: the first two generated tokens carry the excess of the SAE rows (SAE at block 2: 0.958 against 0.135 in tokens 17-32; first token 1.80 in the mean, 0.48 in the median; SAE at block 14: 1.37), while the noise rows show no such start (0.11 and 0.24 at the first token).

findings.claim: What a careful one-paragraph summary for the user should say about H1 and H2
findings.evidence: Built from the findings above. Every figure in it is one I recomputed or one confirmed by Recomputation A or B.
findings.fix: H1 (every normally trained network has built its own small UFO). Not confirmed, and in the paper's sense it cannot be confirmed at run time, because the paper's UFO is a second network that acts only during training. For a weaker form speaks one result: training gave Qwen3-1.7B something the untrained network does not have. The MLPs of blocks 1 to 16 write against any vector that is added to the stream, with about 20 % of the vector per block and about 11 % along the few hundred directions in which real states vary most (untrained network: 0.000). Against reading this as an organiser: it is linear and unspecific; it does not bring the state back (after every block the deviation is larger than the vector that was added); a direction inside the data subspace is treated like one outside unless it is one of the high-variance directions; and by the paper's own measure the two-dimensional share of the MLP activations (31 to 40 % in blocks 0 to 8) is prompt length and question family. Not tested: whether ordinary training lowers the loss of a UFO that only watches (possible in the toy model only), a task that meets the paper's conditions (the addition grid was still running), the same measure in the untrained model, and any second model, so nothing can be said about 'every' network. H2 (an SAE alongside the network in real time, mostly at the lowest layer; does the network brake large disturbances?). For: of the five sites tested, block 0 is where the SAE costs least (0.066 nats per token, top token unchanged at 89 % of positions) and where its error does no more harm than noise of the same size; an SAE that only adds the difference between a modified and the unmodified reconstruction adds no error while it changes nothing; in one loop run (12 prompts, 32 generated tokens, greedy) the distance to the undisturbed model per token did not grow. Against: no brake was found for single disturbances between 0.03 and 1 state norm (the erasure per unit falls with size, the damage grows with the square of the size or faster); the erasure halves the damage only for low-variance vectors added at block 2 and does nothing for content-like vectors at block 14, and an SAE's own error is content-like there; one and the same vector at all positions costs 1.3 to 2.3 times more than independent noise, and an SAE's error is of that systematic kind; used as a filter the SAE does more harm than the noise it was meant to remove at blocks 2 and 14 (1.6 to 1.7 and 3.9 to 4.5 times), and at block 0 it breaks even for one kind of noise and loses for the other (1.5 times); equal noise is not better tolerated at the lowest blocks; and in the loop run the text departed from the undisturbed text in all 12 prompts for every SAE row. Not tested: the communication itself (the SAE changing a feature and writing it back), SAEs trained on this chat model below block 21 (all numbers for the low blocks use SAEs of the base model), texts longer than 64 tokens, sampling, more than one SAE site, disturbances larger than one state norm, and a second model. All of this comes from one model, 16 texts (12 for the SAE runs) and one or two draws of directions; a second draw moved single damage values by up to 22 %.
